translationRepairs: Yet if orders are sent in advance so that preparations can be made, however arduous provisioning may be, how could it drive men to abandon their posts?
Yet if orders are sent in advance so that preparations can be made, however arduous provisioning may be, how could it drive men to throw away their lives?
捐僨 in 何至捐僨 means sacrifice/perish; preceding 自戕 shows the magistrates died, so “abandon their posts” is wrong and “throw away their lives” is accurate.
Yet if proclamations are sent in advance so that preparations may be made, though provisioning is arduous, how could it come to abandoning one's post?
Yet if proclamations are sent in advance so that preparations may be made, though provisioning is arduous, how could it come to men perishing?
Same 捐僨: the literal’s “abandoning one’s post” misreads a lethal sense confirmed by 自戕; “men perishing” matches the Chinese.
When officials caught a thief, he claimed to be connected to the household of Sun Kewang, Prince of Yi, for whom he had bought horses, with a Bordered White Banner bondservant acting as go-between.
When officials caught a thief, he claimed to belong to the household of Sun Kewang, Prince of Yi, in connection with horse-buying, with a Bordered White Banner bondservant acting as go-between.
自列…家人，為買馬 identifies the thief as a household member in a horse-buying matter; “for whom he had bought horses” invents a benefactive the Chinese does not fix.
Before long, Hanlin chancellor Kullene impeached Degele for privately altering the Veritable Records and for promoting each other with Xu Yuanmeng; the case was sent to the Ministry of Punishments.
Before long, Hanlin chancellor Kullene impeached Degele for privately altering the court diaries and for promoting each other with Xu Yuanmeng; the case was sent to the Ministry of Punishments.
起居注 is the court diary institution, distinct from 實錄 (Veritable Records); “court diaries” is the correct rendering.

Before long, Hanlin chancellor Kullene impeached Degele for privately altering the Veritable Records and for mutually promoting each other with Xu Yuanmeng; the case was sent to the Ministry of Punishments to determine guilt.

Before long, Hanlin chancellor Kullene impeached Degele for privately altering the court diaries and for mutually promoting each other with Xu Yuanmeng; the case was sent to the Ministry of Punishments to determine guilt.
Literal likewise misrenders 起居注 as Veritable Records; “court diaries” is correct.
By precedent the Veritable Records went through many drafts before registration; what Degele had altered were not yet finalized drafts.
By precedent the court diaries went through many drafts before registration; what Degele had altered were not yet finalized drafts.
s0114’s 起居注 again denotes court diaries, not Veritable Records; the proposed correction is accurate.
By precedent the Veritable Records were revised through many drafts before being entered in the register; what Degele had deleted and altered were in fact not yet finalized drafts.
By precedent the court diaries were revised through many drafts before being entered in the register; what Degele had deleted and altered were in fact not yet finalized drafts.
Literal of s0114 repeats the 起居注/實錄 error; “court diaries” is correct.
Huguang Governor Zhang Han was a protégé of Grand Secretary Mingzhu; relying on his power he was greedy and violent, and no censor dared expose him.
Huguang Governor Zhang Qian was a protégé of Grand Secretary Mingzhu; relying on his power he was greedy and violent, and no censor dared expose him.
張汧’s given name 汧 is Qian, not Han; Zhang Qian is the correct personal name.
Huguang Governor Zhang Han was a protégé of Grand Secretary Mingzhu; relying on his power he was greedy and violent, and no one on the remonstrance track dared expose him.
Huguang Governor Zhang Qian was a protégé of Grand Secretary Mingzhu; relying on his power he was greedy and violent, and no one on the remonstrance track dared expose him.
Literal likewise mistranslates 汧 as Han; Qian is required.

In the twenty-sixth year Zizhi memorialized to impeach him, stating: "Han has not long held his post, yet he is corrupt in many ways; he extorts every local salt franchise, money bureau, and ferry landing, even levying money by count on shop signs in Hankou market.

In the twenty-sixth year Zizhi memorialized to impeach him, stating: "Qian has not long held his post, yet he is corrupt in many ways; he extorts every local salt franchise, money bureau, and ferry landing, even levying money by count on shop signs in Hankou market.
Short form 汧 in the memorial must be Qian, not Han.

In the twenty-sixth year Zizhi memorialized to impeach him, stating: "Han has not long held his post, yet his corrupt taking of goods has many forms; every local salt franchise, money bureau, and ferry landing he extorts without exception, even to the point of levying money by count on shop signs in Hankou market.

In the twenty-sixth year Zizhi memorialized to impeach him, stating: "Qian has not long held his post, yet his corrupt taking of goods has many forms; every local salt franchise, money bureau, and ferry landing he extorts without exception, even to the point of levying money by count on shop signs in Hankou market.
Literal short form of 汧 must be Qian, not Han.
The emperor stripped Han of office and dispatched Zhili Governor Yu Chenglong, Shanxi Governor Ma Qi, and Vice Censor-in-Chief Kai Yinbu to investigate.
The emperor stripped Qian of office and dispatched Zhili Governor Yu Chenglong, Shanxi Governor Ma Qi, and Vice Censor-in-Chief Kai Yinbu to investigate.
奪汧官 refers to Qian; English Han is a continuing mistranslation.
The emperor ordered Han stripped of office and dispatched Zhili Governor Yu Chenglong, Shanxi Governor Ma Qi, and Vice Censor-in-Chief Kai Yinbu to investigate and try the case.
The emperor ordered Qian stripped of office and dispatched Zhili Governor Yu Chenglong, Shanxi Governor Ma Qi, and Vice Censor-in-Chief Kai Yinbu to investigate and try the case.
Literal of 奪汧官 must use Qian, not Han.
He again told the court that Han was greedy yet no one dared speak, while Zizhi alone impeached him, and immediately granted him promotion within the capital.
He again told the court that Qian was greedy yet no one dared speak, while Zizhi alone impeached him, and immediately granted him promotion within the capital.
謂汧貪婪 again uses given name 汧 = Qian.
He again instructed the court officials, saying that Han was greedy yet no one dared speak, while Zizhi alone was able to impeach him, and immediately granted him promotion within the capital.
He again instructed the court officials, saying that Qian was greedy yet no one dared speak, while Zizhi alone was able to impeach him, and immediately granted him promotion within the capital.
Literal must render 汧 as Qian, not Han.

Chenglong and the others found that as Fujian provincial treasurer Han had covered treasury deficits through subordinates and forcibly collected ninety thousand taels from salt merchants; his superior Zu Zeshen had greedily taken another eighty thousand from the people; the verdict called for strangulation.

Chenglong and the others found that as Fujian provincial treasurer Qian had covered treasury deficits through subordinates and forcibly collected ninety thousand taels from salt merchants; his superior Zu Zeshen had greedily taken another eighty thousand from the people; the verdict called for strangulation.
按得汧以前官 continues the same given name 汧 = Qian.

Chenglong and the others investigated and found that when Han had previously served as Fujian provincial treasurer he had a deficit in the treasury made up by subordinate clerks, and also forcibly collected ninety thousand taels from salt merchants; his superior, Jingnan Circuit Intendant Zu Zeshen, had greedily taken another eighty thousand from the people; when the verdict was submitted the sentence was strangulation.

Chenglong and the others investigated and found that when Qian had previously served as Fujian provincial treasurer he had a deficit in the treasury made up by subordinate clerks, and also forcibly collected ninety thousand taels from salt merchants; his superior, Jingnan Circuit Intendant Zu Zeshen, had greedily taken another eighty thousand from the people; when the verdict was submitted the sentence was strangulation.
Literal of 汧 in the investigation report must be Qian.
Wang Zunxun, Lu Qi, and Ren Chendan, who had recommended Han as governor, were all stripped of office.
Wang Zunxun, Lu Qi, and Ren Chendan, who had recommended Qian as governor, were all stripped of office.
保舉汧為巡撫 uses 汧 = Qian as the recommended person.
Those who had recommended Han as governor—Vice Minister Wang Zunxun, Academician Lu Qi, and Assistant Director of the Court of Judicial Review Ren Chendan—were all punished by loss of office.
Those who had recommended Qian as governor—Vice Minister Wang Zunxun, Academician Lu Qi, and Assistant Director of the Court of Judicial Review Ren Chendan—were all punished by loss of office.
Literal of 保舉汧 must use Qian, not Han.
Governors-general, governors, and military commanders denounce one another with private motives; petty clerks follow suit—how can the people be kept free of litigation?

Governors-general, governors, provincial military commanders, and regional commanders denounce one another with private motives; petty clerks follow suit—how can the people be kept free of litigation?
督、撫、提、鎮 lists four offices; collapsing 提 and 鎮 into one “military commanders” omits the Chinese distinction.
His father was Jia Yu, styled Zuxi.
His father was Jiayu, styled Zuxi.
佳育 is the undivided given name Jiayu; spacing as Jia Yu invents a false two-part English name.
His father Jia Yu, courtesy name Zuxi.
His father was Jiayu, courtesy name Zuxi.
Literal is a fragment and likewise misspaces 佳育; “His father was Jiayu, courtesy name Zuxi.” is grammatical and accurate.
Right Vice Commissioner of Transmission Zhang Yunyi was the son of the late Marquis Yong, who had pacified rebellion.
Right Vice Commissioner of Transmission Zhang Yunyi was the son of Yong, the late Marquis of Pacifying Rebellion.
靖逆侯 is Yong's noble title, not a relative clause about pacifying rebellion. Placing the personal name before the title makes the relationship unambiguous in English.
